items.title: Film Quote of the Day: 'The Departed' Back-and-Forth That Might Be Its Most Underrated
items.summary: I feel like in 2006, people were calling The Departed Scorsese's makeup Oscar for snubs on Goodfellas and Raging Bull, and a few other titles, but the more I watch the movie, the more I think it really has a lot to say about American egos, more than we thought at the time. People usually focus on the loudest moments of the movie, like the literal gunshots, bodies falling, and Jack Nicholson throwing cash around a strip club. It's true that William Monahan’s Oscar-winning script is loaded with iconic lines and actors chewing scenery. But tucked right into the climax is a brief exchange between Matt Damon and Leonardo DiCaprio that hits every note about the theme of the film. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com A Quick Recap of The Departed We're in South Boston, where rookie cop Billy Costigan (Leonardo DiCaprio) is sent undercover to infiltrate the Irish mob syndicate run by the ruthless boss Frank Costello (Jack Nicholson). Unbeknownst to the state police, Costello has placed his own mole, Colin Sullivan (Matt Damon), inside the Special Investigation Unit, where he is mentored by Captain Ellerby (Alec Baldwin) and assigned to track down Costello's informant. Colin uses his access to feed information to Costello, who begins to suspect there is a mole in his unit. At the same time, Billy tries to gain the trust of Costello and his volatile enforcer, French (Ray Winstone). Simultaneously, Billy and Colin are both having affairs with department psychiatrist Madolyn Madden (Vera Farmiga). This is a movie about these two men as mirrors of society and how their society mirrors them, too. It's a cat-and-mouse game that begins under the supervision of Billy's only handlers, Captain Queenan (Martin Sheen) and Sergeant Dignam (Mark Wahlberg), but spirals out of anyone's grasp as the bodies continue to mount and Costello loses all trust in those who surround him. items.title: The Auteur Comeback: Why Movies Feel Like Movies Again
items.summary: Do you remember how fun the press tour for Don't Worry Darling was? Not the movie itself, just the press tour. I recall so vividly how dramatic the red carpet was when the film premiered at Venice, and with this year's Venice just kicking off this week, I was reminded of all that wonderful online discourse. Years later, I'm still quoting star Harry Styles when he talked about working on the film. "My favorite thing about the movie is, like, it feels like a movie. It feels like a real, like, you know, go-to-the-theater-film movie," he said during one press call (via Newsweek). It was not a deep quote or anything, and it was widely memed and mocked. But he is actually saying something here that I and many other cinema fans yearn for in film. I want a movie to feel like a movie. I want it to dredge up all the emotions that a visit to a theater can bring. Sometimes you go to a movie, and it doesn't feel like a movie. Are we back in a time when movies feel like movies? Archer Green on YouTube thinks so. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com Where Are We Now? For years I've been dreaming of a time when indie films and audacious auteurs might be given their flowers and lifted above studio fodder like in ye olden times, aka the 1970s. But check out what's been in theaters in the last couple of years. Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, the first feature shot entirely on IMAX 70mm film. Ryan Coogler's Sinners. Curry Barker's Obsession, a $750,000 horror film that has out-earned almost every low-budget movie in history. Paul Thomas Anderson finally getting a big budget and turning it into One Battle After Another. These are director-driven, big-swing films, and audiences are showing up in ways that don't fit the "superhero fatigue means people are done with theaters" narrative. In the video, Green argues that Hollywood is at a crossroads between films built by directors and films optimized as content. items.title: How Westerns Influenced Modern Visual Storytelling
items.summary: Back in the early days of Hollywood, the Western was the most popular genre. It was a safe bet for making money, but it also became a place where directors and cinematographers could experiment with different visuals within the safety of a money-making venture. So when you're watching a modern Marvel movie or something else, and they cut to a wide shot, a close-up, or a day-for-night, you should thank a Western. Now, there were people experiencing all over the world, and a lot of our modern influences come from a homogenization of film language over the first 50 years of movies, but this is a post about how the Western greatly influences all of that. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com Landscape as Character This is the big one, and while you may have early movies that did this kind of thing, it was cemented into Hollywood by the Western. Before John Ford dragged a crew out to Monument Valley for Stagecoach (1939), cinema was made on sound stages where the sun was a light and the moon a source card. Getting out of the booth and into the real world gave each location a personality. Ford understood that the environment could carry as much emotional and narrative weight as any line of dialogue, so he made sure to use it ot highlight themes of isolation, adventure, and even endless possibilities. This also gave us some visual shorthand for the man vs. nature conflict. I like to think the Extreme Wide Shot evolved from those western vistas, too. And what about internal framing? Think about the famous opening and closing shots of The Searchers (1956), where we see John Wayne through a dark doorway looking out into the sun-drenched desert, which instantly communicates that he is an outsider doomed to roam the wilderness.
